findings.title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, so every instance shares the same timestamp
findings.body:
`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain dataclass default. It is computed once, when the class body runs at module import, not on each instantiation.

Every `AssignmentSource` built without an explicit `queued` (including all those from `from_integration`) gets the worker process's import time. In a long-lived worker that can be hours or days stale. Any current or future use of `queued` for staleness, ordering or debouncing of rapid assignee changes (the scenario this PR targets) will be wrong.

Use `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

`test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it cannot catch this.

findings.title: `to_dict` puts a raw `datetime` into Celery task kwargs; the round-trip is not type-safe
findings.body:
`to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which contains a `datetime` object. That dict is passed as `assignment_source_dict` to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`.

Task payloads should be JSON-safe primitives. Under a JSON serializer the datetime is either rejected at enqueue time or converted to an ISO string. `from_dict` does `cls(**input_dict)` with no type coercion, so after the round-trip `queued` silently becomes a `str` despite its `datetime` annotation.

Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()` or epoch) in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict`.

findings.title: Cycle guard compares integration IDs, so syncs to other linked issues in the same integration are dropped
findings.body:
`should_sync` returns False whenever `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`. The outbound task runs once per linked `ExternalIssue`.

If a Sentry group is linked to two issues in the same Jira integration (A and B), an inbound change on A now blocks the outbound update to B as well. Previously B would be kept in sync; this is a silent regression.

The loop being fixed is between Sentry and the specific external issue that sent the webhook. Carrying the originating external issue key/id in `AssignmentSource` and skipping only that issue would break the cycle without suppressing legitimate propagation.

findings.title: `from_dict` silently returns None on malformed input, which re-enables the sync loop
findings.body:
`from_dict` catches `ValueError`/`TypeError` and returns None without logging. In `sync_assignee_outbound`, a None source means `should_sync` skips the cycle check and proceeds with the outbound sync.

Any schema drift in the payload (an added or renamed field, or tasks enqueued by a different code version during deploy) silently brings back the exact cycle this PR fixes. Log or emit a metric when parsing fails so this is observable.

findings.title: `sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter that nothing passes or honors
findings.body:
The abstract signature of `sync_status_outbound` now declares `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`. No caller supplies it, no implementation uses it, and the status outbound path does not consult the source in `should_sync`.

This suggests to readers and implementers that status-sync cycles are also prevented when they are not. Either wire it through the status sync path or remove it from this PR.

findings.title: No test that a different integration still receives the sync, or that the inbound path breaks the cycle
findings.body:
The new test only covers the case where the source matches the target integration and the outbound call is skipped.

Two behaviors are untested:
- An `AssignmentSource` from a different integration still triggers `sync_assignee_outbound` on the linked integration.
- `sync_group_assignee_inbound` (the real webhook entry point) does not call back out to the originating integration.

The existing inbound tests run without `self.tasks()` and without mocking outbound, so the end-to-end cycle break is not verified.
